title: Lior and the Room
premise: Noor Fairweather, a nonbinary substitute teacher, arrives in the fading town of Hollowmere where students have been vanishing from classroom photographs for fifty years. When old family photos begin showing an extra chair that no one owns, Noor learns their grandmother was one of four children who took something from the school in 1974—a ledger of names the town used to 'unwrite' unwanted kids. As the harvest moon approaches and the unwritten grow bolder, Noor must return the ledger to the room beneath the school where it was taken, choosing justice outside the law over the town's comfortable silence. In the end, Noor reads every stolen name aloud, restoring the missing children to memory even as the town's founders crumble into dust.
about_author: Zephyrine Vane is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent a decade collecting local legends about vanished students. They write quiet horror about institutions that forget on purpose, and live somewhere with too many doors.

chapters.title: The Counted Doors
chapters.summary: POV: Noor. Noor arrives in Hollowmere to substitute for a teacher who 'resigned,' immediately unsettled by the principal's ritual of counting doors each evening and by a classroom photo with an empty space no one will explain. The emotional beat is wary displacement—Noor, used to being invisible themselves, recognizes the practiced art of looking away.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: POV: Noor. Sorting grandma Edith's attic, Noor finds decades of family photos, each now containing a plain wooden chair that wasn't there before—and in the oldest, someone's silhouette seated in it. The beat is creeping dread: the past is rearranging itself around Noor, and it seems to want a place at the table.

chapters.title: The Missing-Class Problem
chapters.summary: POV: Noor. A student named Wren tells Noor about 'the roster that loses people'—kids whose names vanish from attendance and memory alike, starting in 1974. Noor checks the archives and finds Edith's name inked out. The beat is righteous anger kindling into purpose; invisibility, Noor realizes, was never chosen—it was imposed.

chapters.title: What Edith Kept
chapters.summary: POV: Noor, with letters from Edith. Edith's letters confess that she and three friends stole a ledger from the school in 1974—the book the founding families used to unwrite troublesome children—and hid it rather than burn it, out of fear. The beat is inherited guilt; Noor understands the chair is a summons from someone Edith failed to save.

chapters.title: The Founders' Benevolence
chapters.summary: POV: Noor. The town's oldest family, the Merricks, welcome Noor warmly while subtly warning them off the school's lower floor. Noor notices the same faces across fifty years of photos, unchanged. The beat is the horror of polite menace—belonging in Hollowmere is offered only to those who agree not to remember.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: POV: Noor. The moon swells and the unwritten become visible at dusk: pale figures in the schoolyard, watching windows. Wren's name begins fading from the roster. The beat is urgency and protectiveness—Noor, who finally belongs somewhere, watches belonging get revoked in real time.

chapters.title: Four Children, One Promise
chapters.summary: POV: Noor. Following Edith's clues, Noor finds the ledger hidden in the walls of grandma's house, wrapped in a child's coat. Reading it, they hear whispers of every unwritten name. The beat is grief transformed into resolve: returning the book isn't enough—it must be read aloud, all of it, before moonrise.

chapters.title: The Room Beneath
chapters.summary: POV: Noor. On the night before the harvest moon, Noor descends into the sealed room under the school, where the chair waits and the walls are papered with attendance sheets. The Merricks arrive to stop them, revealing the unwriting continues today. The beat is confrontation—justice versus law, with Noor refusing both the town's silence and its permission.

chapters.title: Every Name Aloud
chapters.summary: POV: Noor. Under the full harvest moon, Noor reads the ledger cover to cover as the founders unravel and the unwritten step forward out of half-existence, each named and witnessed. Wren's name re-inks itself. The beat is cathartic climax—memory as restitution, voice as the only lawful thing left.

chapters.title: A Place at the Table
chapters.summary: POV: Noor. Weeks later, Hollowmere remembers imperfectly but honestly; a memorial plaque lists the lost, and the extra chair remains in Edith's photos—now empty, at peace. Noor accepts a permanent post and sets a fifth chair in their classroom. The beat is earned belonging: identity affirmed, justice kept, doors left open.
